text: Group project, due Thursday. Four names on the shared file, one cursor blinking: yours. Nobody else has even opened it.
Your report card is stuck to the fridge with a pineapple magnet. You didn't put it there. Someone in this house did.
The dentist taps your teeth with a little mirror and says the word: braces. Two years of metal.
You're reading aloud in class and your voice cracks mid-word, high like a kettle. Thirty heads turn. Someone snorts.
Your parents finally hand you a phone. It comes with a printed list of rules, two pages long, signed by both of them.
The class group chat is roasting a kid who isn't in it. Forty messages, crying-laughing faces. Your thumb hovers.
Your weekly screen time report pops up: nine hours a day. That's longer than school. That's longer than sleep.
You have a crush. You know because their name is in your notebook margin. Twice. Once inside a small, wobbly heart.
School dance. The gym smells of floor wax and body spray. Your crush is standing alone by the crisps, holding a cup.
You spent forty minutes writing that message. Your crush replied in four seconds with just "lol". Nothing else.
Your sibling took your hoodie and your charger. Without asking. You can see the hoodie right now. They're wearing it.
Past midnight, the back window slides open. Your sibling climbs in, shoes in hand, and freezes when they see you.
Family dinner. Phones go in the basket by the door. Yours buzzes in there twice, face down, like it's calling for help.
Your parents are arguing in the next room again. The words are muffled, but the tone isn't. A cupboard door slams.
A new kid moved in down the street. You've seen them twice, sitting on the wall alone, kicking it with one heel.
Your oldest friend has a new group now. You see the photos: all of them at the park, on a Saturday. You weren't invited.
Sleepover. Someone puts on a horror film you're far too young for. The lights are off and the first scream is a doll.
Exams start Monday. It is Friday night. Your textbook is still in its plastic wrap, and your friends are going out.
After class, a teacher keeps you back. Not to tell you off. To say you have a real gift for their subject. You blush.
Detention. The only other kid there is the scariest kid in school. They're carving something into the desk with a key.
A spot has appeared on the tip of your nose overnight. It's red, it's shiny, and today is school picture day.
A video says you need a ten-step skincare routine. Serums, toners, a tiny jade roller. Your face currently uses soap.
You grew so fast this term that your trousers now stop above your ankles. Your socks are on full public display.
There's an old guitar at the back of the cupboard, under the coats. Five strings, a sticker of a star. Nobody plays it.
You filled a whole sketchbook in a month. Hands, dogs, your teacher as a frog. Some of them are actually good.
Try-outs for the school team are tomorrow after lunch. Your kit is by the door. Your stomach is in knots.
You ask for more pocket money. Your parent puts down their mug, looks at you over their glasses, and asks what for.
You find a wallet on the bus seat next to you. It's fat with cash. There's a photo of a smiling dog inside too.
A birthday card arrives from a relative you've met twice. Inside: a crisp note and "Don't spend it all at once".
You wake up with a fever on a school day. A real one this time. The thermometer agrees. Your pillow is soaked.
Everyone at school is drinking energy drinks. The cans are neon. One kid says he hasn't blinked since Tuesday.
Your favourite band is playing in the city next month. You've asked your parents. They said "maybe". It means no.
The family is driving eight hours to visit relatives. You're in the back with a cool box and a bag of boiled sweets.
A goat is standing in your front garden, eating the hedge. Nobody on the street owns a goat. It looks at you, chewing.
There's a rumour going round about you. It isn't true. Kids stop talking when you walk past. One of them giggles.
You're old enough for a learner permit now. The handbook is two hundred pages of road signs and stopping distances.
First driving lesson. You haven't left the drive yet. Your parent in the passenger seat is gripping it like a ride.
Parallel parking. Attempt number seven. The car behind you has stopped to watch. Somebody on the pavement is filming.
Driving test day. The examiner has a clipboard and hasn't smiled once. They write something down before you start.
You ask to borrow the car for the night. Your parent looks at the keys, then at you, then at the keys again.
A friend with a brand-new licence offers you a lift. Seven people, five seats. Someone is already lying across the back.
Final exams in a month. Your future, apparently, depends on it. Every teacher says so. The calendar on the wall agrees.
Time to choose your subjects. The form is due Friday. Your parents have opinions and have printed them out for you.
Someone in a chat is selling the exam answers. Screenshots, a price, a promise. Three people have already paid.
An essay is due at 9 a.m. It's midnight. The page is white and the cursor blinks at you like it's judging.
Open day at a faraway college. Old stone buildings, a lake, students reading on the grass. It looks amazing.
There's a scholarship that covers almost everything. The essay question is three words: "Who are you?" You stare.
Your crush stops by your locker and asks if you're going to the party on Saturday. Your brain goes completely blank.
First date at the diner. You've counted your coins twice. You have enough money for exactly one milkshake.
Your parents want to meet the person you're seeing. Your mum has already asked what they like to eat. Twice.
They broke up with you. By text. It ended with a full stop. You read it eleven times on the bathroom floor.
Party at a house where the parents are away for the weekend. You can hear the bass from the end of the street.
At the party, someone hands you a red cup. The drink is a colour you can't name. You don't know what's in it.
A photo of you mid-sneeze is going round the school. Eyes shut, mouth wide. Someone has added sound effects.
One of your videos got ten thousand views overnight. Your phone won't stop buzzing. Strangers are quoting you.
Your best friend is moving away at the end of the year. They told you on the swings, staring at their shoes.
Your friend goes quiet, then tells you something they've never told anyone. Their hands are shaking a little.
Your younger sibling is failing maths. You've seen the test in the bin, folded small. They won't ask for help.
A parent lost their job. Money is tight at home. The heating stays off and the shopping is mostly own-brand now.
You're home an hour after curfew. You turn into the street and see it: every light in the house is still on.
You catch yourself in the shop window and decide, right there, to get fit. Your trainers are still in the box.
It's 3 a.m. and you're still scrolling. You've watched a man restore a rusty axe. Then another one. Then a third.
You want to dye your hair a colour that doesn't occur in nature. Electric teal. The box is in your basket already.
You've saved up a decent amount from shifts and birthdays. It's sitting there in your account, looking at you.
A text says you won a brand new tablet. Just pay a small fee to claim it. The link has a lot of numbers in it.
The animal shelter needs weekend volunteers. On the poster, a one-eyed dog looks straight into your soul.
Students are walking out of class at ten o'clock for a cause you care about. The clock says nine fifty-eight.
The end-of-year dance is in two weeks. Everyone's talking outfits. You have one shirt and it has a stain on it.
Everyone keeps asking what you'll do after school. Aunts, teachers, the dentist. Even the dentist wants to know.
A raccoon is sitting at the kitchen table like it lives here. It has its little hands on the fruit bowl. It stares.
A wisdom tooth is coming in sideways. Your whole jaw aches. You've been chewing on one side of your mouth for days.
First night in juvie. The door locks from the outside with a heavy clunk. The mattress is thin and smells of bleach.
Your roommate wants your pudding cup. Every day. Today they just sit and watch you peel the lid back, slowly.
There's school in juvie too. Bolted-down desks, old textbooks. The teacher looks tired but kind, and learns your name.
Visiting day. Your family came. They brought the good biscuits, chocolate on both sides. Mum's eyes are red.
Your caseworker signs the form with a cheap pen and slides it over. You're going home. Your bag is already packed.
The job application has a box near the bottom: "Have you ever been convicted?" It's very small. It feels huge.
Your parents check your room now. And your phone. And your shoes. Last night they checked inside your pillowcase.
The overseas school trip needs a police check. Everyone else's came back clean. Yours comes back flagged in red.
You're 18, and the money is yours now. No allowance, no one checking. So what kind of person are you with money?
Your first election. The polling station is a school hall that smells of floor polish. The pencil is on a string.
One red sock got into the wash. Now everything you own has turned pink. Your work shirts. Your towels. Your socks.
You're renting now. A parent calls to ask if you're eating vegetables. There's a single sad onion in your fridge.
Your flatmate's dishes have been in the sink for nine days. Something is growing. It has a texture. It may have plans.
The landlord wants to keep your deposit for a scuff on the wall. That scuff was there when you moved in. You're sure.
There's black mould behind the wardrobe, spreading up the wall like a map. You've been breathing it for a while.
You're still in your childhood bedroom. Single bed, old posters. The glow stars on the ceiling still glow.
Your first real interview. The interviewer clicks her pen and asks where you see yourself in five years.
The application wants two years' experience you don't have. It would only take one little line. Nobody checks, right?
A stranger online can double your money in a week. There are testimonials, a countdown timer and a very nice logo.
At the till, the shop assistant offers you a store card. Ten percent off today! She's already reaching for the form.
The old car coughs and dies at a junction. Hazards on. Everyone behind you has an opinion, and a horn to share it.
You've had a few, and your car is right there in the car park. It's only ten minutes. The keys are in your hand.
Someone in the club toilets leans over and offers you a small bag. "You'll love it." The bass thuds through the wall.
Your head is a bass drum, your mouth tastes of carpet, and work starts in forty minutes. The light hurts.
A gym offers you a year's membership at a launch price. Mirrors, machines, a smoothie bar. You feel a new you coming on.
You've eaten instant noodles for eleven days in a row. You've started ranking the flavours. Chicken is winning.
There's a mole on your back that looks different from how you remember it. Darker, maybe. Bigger, maybe.
You've been tired for months. Coffee does nothing. This morning you cried at a bus timetable. It wasn't even late.
The group chat from school has gone quiet. The last message is a thumbs-up from four months ago. Nobody's posted since.
A friend asks to borrow $1,000. They swear it's only until Friday. They don't say which Friday. They look desperate.
Someone your age is getting married. Already. The invite has gold edges, and the gift list starts at $150.
Your friends are going travelling for a year. Beaches, night buses, cheap hostels. There's a spare bunk for you.
It's 1am, the neon sign says open, and the tattoo place smells of ink and antiseptic. Your friend knows a guy.
You could sell stuff online at weekends. Old clothes, flipped furniture. Everyone on the internet says it's easy.
A brown envelope from the tax office lands on the mat. Nothing good has ever come in brown. It feels thick.
Someone from your school just bought a house. Keys, big smile, the lot. You just bought a slightly nicer sponge.
The food bank down the road is short of hands on Saturdays. The queue outside goes past the bakery now.
Your grandparent wants help with their phone. Again. It's the same button. They're holding the phone upside down.
A pigeon has walked into your flat through the balcony door. It sits on the sofa like it's paying rent. It isn't.
A form asks for your "next of kin". You have to look up what that means. Then you sit with the pen for a while.
A teacher reads your surname off the register and sighs. 'I taught the last one of you. And the one before.'
'Your family has always done well,' says the careers teacher, looking at your marks over her glasses. 'Until now.'
The portrait of the one who left you everything hangs in the hall. The eyes follow you. So does the disappointment.
In a drawer: the family watch. It stopped the minute its last owner did. A dealer turns it over and offers $4,000.
A cousin you've never met says the will was wrong and wants their share. They've brought a folder. It's colour-coded.
The family plot at the cemetery has one space left. The office rings, very cheerful, to ask if you'd like to reserve it.
Every year your family eats the same grey pudding on the same day. Nobody likes it. This year it's your turn to make it.
On an old door frame, a parent's height marks in pencil, year by year. At your age they were taller. By a lot.
An old neighbour tells you your family is cursed: not one of you has ever died peacefully. She says it kindly, with tea.
In the attic: a letter marked 'to be opened when I am gone'. You open it, heart racing. It is mostly about the boiler.
A relative has heard you came into money. They have a business idea and a slideshow. It involves alpacas. Many alpacas.
A website offers to trace your family tree for $200. The ad says one in five people find a pirate. Or worse.
Family reunion. Forty relatives, one barbecue, paper plates, and an uncle with opinions and a folding chair.
A man at a market stall sells you your family crest. It has a lion on it. Nobody in your family has ever met a lion.
A local historian wants to write a book about your family. Pen ready, they ask if there's anything you'd like left out.
The council offers a bench with your family name on it for $900. You're not dead, but they suggest planning ahead.
